title: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Where organisms compete most closely, as on a small patch of ground, the advantages of diversification mean that the coexisting inhabitants generally belong to different genera and orders.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: where they come into the closest competition with each other, the advantages of diversification of structure, with the accompanying differences of habit and constitution, determine that the inhabitants, which thus jostle each other most closely, shall, as a general rule, belong to what we call different genera and orders.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation”. Scope: small-area communities, e.g. turf plots, islets, small ponds

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-21: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Taxonomic dispersion in local communities is directly measurable with broad public data and standard null models. The empirical generalization can be resolved even though its proposed competitive explanation is less secure.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare observed genus- and order-level diversity within standardized small plots to null communities preserving richness and regional species pools. Consistent phylogenetic overdispersion and higher coexistence among distant taxa support the claim; clustering or null structure refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Plot grain and regional-pool choice affect null-model results.

Co-occurrence does not prove that listed organisms compete most closely.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.86

discriminating power: 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Plot data and phylogenies make a null-model test of coexistence and relatedness straightforward for plants. The claim's small-area scope is well matched by vegetation plots and poorly matched for animals. Rank names are arbitrary and filtering is a serious alternative, so the result would be informative for plants and would still need the null model spelled out in the design.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In small plots, compare the mean taxonomic or phylogenetic distance of co-occurring species with draws from the regional species pool. Excess membership in different genera and orders, relative to that null, would confirm the claim; co-occurrence as related as the null, or more related, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Without a regional null, any diverse plot belongs to multiple genera by arithmetic.

sPlot access is restricted, and animal assemblages are poorly represented relative to plants.

Habitat filtering can increase relatedness and offset a competition effect.

operationalizability: 0.76
discriminating power: 0.52
data adequacy: 0.5
